summary: This note explains the formal and practical leadership roles in the United States Senate. The Vice President is the constitutional President of the Senate and the President pro tempore is the constitutional leader in the Vice President's absence, but neither usually presides daily. Instead, junior majority-party senators preside, and the Majority Leader in practice manages the chamber, unlike the House where the Speaker holds significant discretionary power. The note also gives the Senate's current partisan composition.
one_line: Explains why the Senate Majority Leader, not the Vice President or President pro tempore, practically runs the U.S. Senate, and how it differs from the House Speaker's role.
key_facts: The Constitution designates the Vice President of the United States as President of the United States Senate.
The Constitution calls for a President pro tempore to lead the Senate when the Vice President is absent.
The President pro tempore is customarily the most senior (longest-serving) Senator in the majority party.
Neither the Vice President nor the President pro tempore actually presides over the Senate on a daily basis.
Daily presiding duties are given to junior Senators of the majority party.
The Vice President may belong to a different party than the Senate majority and is not a member subject to discipline.
The Senate's rules of procedure give the presiding officer very little power beyond the presiding role.
The Majority Leader is the person who, in practice, manages the Senate.
In the House of Representatives, the elected Speaker has a great deal of discretionary power.
The House Speaker generally presides over votes on bills.
The Senate is currently composed of 51 Republicans, 47 Democrats, and 2 independents.
The 2 independent senators both caucus with the Democrats.
